title: The Epic and the Unoccupied Garden
summary: A peace negotiator’s protected zone, a founding ruler’s evolving epic, and a naval trade reversal converge in a disputed upland valley.
history: An upland founder’s life survived through performed epic alongside sparse independent records. Later households used the epic to justify incompatible claims to a fertile valley. In 779 a negotiator established a garden zone from which armed officers withdrew for talks, hoping protected meeting space would end recurring conflict. Outside coalitions continued contesting its borders and access. A naval battle far downstream redirected trade, weakening sponsors who had supplied the negotiations and strengthening new patrons. The peace zone became both a genuine refuge and a place where rivals accumulated influence. Present gardeners compare heroic memory, signed terms, and changed supply routes to preserve talks without pretending withdrawal of one force made the valley free of coercion.
question: whether the meeting garden can remain protected when the trade revenues supporting its food and repairs now pass through rival downstream hands.
transformations: A peace process and a withdrawn-force negotiating zone become a protected garden whose practical dependencies remain contested.
A founding ruler preserved through oral epic and later corroborating records becomes layered memory rather than literal reproduction of a real epic.
A naval victory redirecting established trade becomes a downstream battle affecting sponsors; modern naval technology is excluded.
A fertile region divided among competing powers becomes overlapping claims whose residents’ needs exceed the positions of outside rulers.
rows: Pastren of the Meeting Garden

Pastren withdrew officers to create negotiating space but left uncertain who would inspect armed visitors. His hope was genuine and incomplete. Later accounts must preserve both, because the zone’s failures arose partly from practical terms its ideal language omitted.
The Unoccupied Garden

The garden contains cultivated paths and pomegranate shade rather than empty neutral ground. Local households maintain it. Calling it unoccupied concealed their work and claims, making a peace image dependent on people the negotiations initially treated as scenery.
The Valley Epic Keepers

Keepers perform variant lives of the founder and identify their teaching lineages. Outside claimants want one fixed version supporting exclusive title. The group preserves variation beside corroborating records, refusing to make a meaningful epic an automatic cadastral map.
The Downstream Fleet Reversal

A coalition fleet lost control of a key harbor and trade shifted toward victors’ landings. Valley sponsors lost revenue before negotiators revised budgets. The peace garden’s shortages therefore originated far beyond the speeches and patrols visible within its borders.
The Founder’s Unverified Saddle

The saddle is old and repeatedly repaired, but no custody chain links it securely to the epic ruler. Keepers label the uncertainty. Its teaching use remains valuable without demanding that every cherished object authenticate the most prestigious possible owner.
The Variant Spoken First

Performers identify which epic version they will use before reciting. Listeners can compare without interrupting every line. The custom protects art’s continuity while preventing a chosen variant from silently presenting itself as the only history ever remembered.
The Founder Beyond the Epic

The booklet compares oral episodes with independent travel and tribute records. Some details align and others remain unconfirmed. Readers preserve that pattern, allowing historical existence to be established without requiring every dramatic event to become literal fact.
The Garden Border Hoopoe

Hoopoes nest across political boundary markers and feed in cultivated beds. Patrols clear vegetation to improve sightlines. Gardeners negotiate narrow inspection paths, preserving habitat and crops while addressing real safety needs without stripping the whole meeting place bare.
The Negotiators’ Food Road

The road connects kitchens to talks through several disputed jurisdictions. Each claims inspection rights. Finite passage agreements keep food moving, showing that a protected meeting depends on many modest commitments outside the apparently neutral room.
The Resident Within Neutrality

A peace zone must recognize residents’ cultivation and custody even when armed authorities withdraw. The clause prevents neutral language from erasing ordinary land relations. It protects useful talks without pretending hosts surrendered every right by welcoming them.
Sundren of the Returning Epic

Sundren’s remembered rise became a model for dispossessed rulers. Independent records establish authority but not every hardship later singers attach to him. Present teachers preserve inspiration while distinguishing narrative identification from proof of a specific present inheritance.
The Harbor That Fed the Talks

The harbor once supplied grain cheaply and now pays victorious toll houses. Its inhabitants need trade and resent the new terms. Their accounts connect naval change to inland hunger, making geography a lived chain of costs rather than separate military and diplomatic histories.
The Protected Garden Hosts

Hosts welcome opposing delegates and retain their own planting schedules. Negotiators demand constant availability. Finite hosting terms protect crops and rest, preserving hospitality against the idea that peace’s importance authorizes unlimited unpaid service.
The First Withdrawal Ceremony

Officers left amid public applause, but visitors continued arriving armed under different credentials. The ceremony achieved a real reduction in one force. Inspection records reveal why that achievement could not substitute for the broader access rules the garden still needed.
The Peace Table Grain Cup

The cup measures food supplied per delegate and exposes expensive entourages. Patrons call counting inhospitable. Hosts explain that accounting makes continued welcome possible, preventing a prestigious meeting from exhausting the households whose generosity sustains it.
The Epic’s Unchosen Listener

Listeners may decline a version without losing access to garden meals. Claimant rulers object that refusal insults ancestral authority. The practice keeps performance from manufacturing consent, especially where an epic is being used to support disputed title.
The Naval Toll’s Inland Costs

The account follows increased harbor fees through transport, kitchens, and negotiating budgets. It documents concrete effects without claiming the battle explains every valley conflict. Trade change becomes one important dependency among several, not a universal historical cause.
The Founder’s Empty Reins

Stored reins tighten briefly near a basin when promised host provisions fail. Leather contraction explains ordinary tension. The unresolved recurrence remains limited to the hosting pledge, preventing an evocative relic from deciding every claimant’s version of the founder’s will.
Peace Garden Cultivation

Gardeners schedule harvest around talks while reserving time for pruning and channel work. Sponsors fund impressive meeting tents more readily. Public accounts make maintenance visible, keeping peace’s setting alive rather than sacrificing cultivation to its ceremonial image.
The Garden’s New Sponsor

A victorious downstream house offers food in exchange for privileged access. Hosts fear losing talks if they refuse. Negotiators seek several bounded contributions, reducing dependence on one patron without pretending the garden can feed everyone through neutrality alone.
